ROLL CALL: At 6:16 p.m., on Monday, September 25, 2023, the Alhambra City Council met in the
Council Chambers of Alhambra City Hall.

PRESENT:  LEE, MALONEY, MAZA
ABSENT:  ANDRADE-STADLER, PÉREZ

Officials Present: City Manager Binnquist, City Attorney Montes, Assistant City Manager Garcia,
Deputy City Manager Stover, City Clerk Myles, Director of Finance Lieu, Director of Parks and
Recreation Macias, Director of Library LohGuan, Director of Community Development Ho, Director of
Human Resources Ko, Chief of Police Kennedy

FLAG SALUTE:  Led by Mayor Maza

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledged that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to prioritize
respect for the historic culture and contemporary presence of the native peoples throughout California,
especially in the greater Los Angeles/Alhambra area. We come with respect and gratitude for the
Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the caretakers of this land. It is through their
examples that we are reminded of our greater responsibility to take care of Mother Earth and to take
care of each other.

READING OF ORDINANCE TITLES

Government Code Section 36934 requires that all ordinances be read in full prior to City Council taking
action on the ordinance. By listing the ordinance title on the Council agenda, Council may determine
that the title has been read.

Action Taken: By motion, determined that the titles to all ordinances which appear on this public
agenda have been read, and waived further reading.

  Ayes:  MALONEY, LEE, MAZA

PRESENTATIONS

1.  CONSIDERATION OF DEADLINE FOR PLANNING COMMISSION TO REVIEW ZONING
  CODE AMENDMENTS – F2M20-37, M2M23-165

  City Attorney MONTES delivered a staff report. At the last City Council meeting, the City
  Council requested that an agenda item be placed on the Council’s agenda to consider setting
  a deadline for the Planning Commission to complete their review of the revisions to the housing
  element and the proposed zoning code amendments. Even though the Planning Commission

  1
9-25-23
   has completed its review of the Housing Element, without the completed zoning code updates,
  HCD will not certify the City’s housing element. Government Code section 65853 provides
  that when a planning commission has not provided a recommendation on a zoning code
  amendment within a reasonable time, the City Council may require by written notice that the
  planning commission make its recommendation to the Council within 40 days. Failure to do
  so shall be deemed a recommendation for approval of the zoning amendment. Staff
  recommends that the Council discuss whether or not to set a deadline for the Planning
  Commission to make a recommendation to the City Council on the zoning code updates
  currently pending before the Planning Commission. If Council decides to set a deadline, staff
  should be directed to transmit that deadline to the Planning Commission in writing.

  Public Comment:
  1) Lewis McCammon, 105 N. Cordova St., discussed the timeline of the housing element and the
  zoning code update and suggested dealing with the housing element first if there is a tight
  deadline.

  Public Comment via Zoom:
  1) Melissa Michaelson, via Zoom, discussed the timeline of the housing element and expressed
  hope that the Council will insist on more thorough revisions of the Housing Element.

  2) Ms. Judy, via Zoom, inquired about the timeline to adopt a revised housing element and zoning
  code.

  Discussion: Councilmember LEE noted that it’s been 30 years since the zoning code has
  been updated, noted that the City is under a time crunch to finish the update, inquired about
  where in the process the updates are currently, inquired why the process has taken over 20
  meetings, and noted that there needs to be a clear timeframe to finish this process. Director
  of Community Development HO responded to questions.

PÉREZ: Vice Mayor PÉREZ entered the meeting at 6:38 p.m.

  Councilmember MALONEY discussed the importance of finishing this process and stated
  there could be penalties from the State if the City does not adopt their housing element in
  time.

  Vice Mayor PÉREZ discussed the current builder’s remedy projects in the City, suggested
  pushing back non-essential items for the Planning Commission so that the housing element
  and zoning code updates can be finished, and noted that she’s in favor of providing the
  community an opportunity for feedback but noted that there is a time crunch to get these
  updates finished.

  Mayor MAZA expressed his appreciation to the Planning Commission for their work on the
  housing element and zoning code updates, discussed the City’s exposure to builder’s remedy
  and the need to get these updates finished.

  The Council continued to discuss a timeline for the City’s housing element and zoning code
  updates and a potential deadline for the Planning Commission to provide a recommendation.

  Action Taken:  City Council provided direction to bring back this item to the October
  23, 2023 meeting and to reconsider it based on where the Planning Commission is in the
  process of the zoning code update and to have staff emphasize importance of moving it
  through the process at the Planning Commission.

 2.  CONSIDERATION OF AN URGENCY INTERIM ZONING ORDINANCE PROHIBITING THE
  ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW FIREARM SALES BUSINESSES; FIRST READING OF AN
  ORDINANCE REQUIRING SAFE STORAGE OF FIREARMS; AND FIRST READING OF AN
  ORDINANCE PROHIBITING THE CARRYING OF FIREARMS ON PUBLICLY OWNED
  PROPERTY AND DETERMINE THAT THESE ACTIONS ARE EXEMPT FROM CEQA –
  F2M23-7, O2M23-4818, O2M23-4819, O2M23-4820

  City Attorney MONTES delivered a staff report. At the September 11, 2023 City Council
  meeting, Vice Mayor Pérez requested that a suite of ordinances recently adopted by the City
  of Monterey Park be presented to the City Council for consideration. The Council concurred
  in agendizing those items for Council consideration. One of the ordinances, a buffer zone
  ordinance, would require a public hearing before the Planning Commission prior to
  consideration by the City Council. In light of the delay that presents for adoption, the Council
  requested an interim urgency ordinance be brought forward for Council’s consideration to
  potentially go into effect pending the preparation of and hearings on a buffer zone ordinance.
  Monterey Park adopted an ordinance that would prohibit the sales of firearms within certain
  areas of the city—those within 1000 feet of sensitive receptors (residences, schools,
  community resource centers). In those areas where firearm sales are allowed, a conditional
  use permit is required in order to ensure that the sale activity does not have negative impacts
  on surrounding uses. Staff intends to study a similar ordinance for Alhambra, which will
  ultimately require a public hearing before the Planning Commission and City Council.
  Government Code Section 65858 allows for the adoption as an urgency measure of interim
  zoning regulations that prohibit certain uses while those are being studied for additional
  regulation. A 4/5 vote of the Council is required to adopt this interim ordinance, which will last
  for a period of 45 days. In order to extend the moratorium, a public hearing must be held, at
  which time the Council can extend the term of the ordinance.

  Additionally, staff has drafted a safe storage ordinance and an ordinance prohibiting firearms
  on City property for Council consideration. The safe storage ordinance would add a new
  section 9.92.050 to the Alhambra Municipal Code entitled “Safe Storage.” The proposed
  ordinance requires any person in a residence within the City to store firearms in a locked
  container or disable them with an appropriate safety device in the home. Keeping a firearm
  locked when it is not being carried prevents unauthorized users, including children, from
  accessing and using firearms which can reduce unintentional discharges, firearm theft, and
  suicide. The proposed ordinance regarding prohibiting guns on City property would prohibit
  (with exceptions for law enforcement personnel) the possession of loaded firearms on any
  City-owned property. That would include, without limitation, persons carrying concealed
  weapons in accordance with valid permits.

  Finally, the City reviewed the environmental impacts of these three Ordinances under the
  California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and
  the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
  Guidelines”). These Ordinances are not subject to further review environmental review
  because: (1) they will not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change
  in the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15060(c)(2); (2) there is no possibility that the
  Ordinances themselves may have a significant effect on the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs.
  § 15061(b)(3)); and (3) the Ordinances, by themselves, do not constitute a “project” as defined
  in the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15378). The Ordinances are for general
  policies and procedure-making. It can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that
  these Ordinances may have a significant effect on the environment.

  Public Comment:

  3
9-25-23
   1) Lewis McCammon, 105 N. Cordova St., expressed support for the item suggested putting
  additional clarification language on what City owned property is in the ordinance.

  2) Katie Chan, Environmental & Sustainability Commissioner, expressed concern with the
  proposed language in the ordinance and stated she did not fell it did enough to prevent gun
  violence but supported the overall ordinance.

  Public Comment via Zoom:
  1) Melissa Michelson, via Zoom, expressed support for the ordinance but stated it did not go far
  enough to protect the community from gun violence and suggested banning all sales of firearms
  in the City.

  Discussion: Vice Mayor PÉREZ inquired about the definition of public spaces in the
  proposed ordinance. City Attorney MONTES provided clarification.

  Councilmember MALONEY expressed support for the urgency ordinance and noted it gives
  the City time to think about what a permanent ordinance would look like.

  Councilmember LEE discussed the importance of educating gun owners of the new
  regulations once these ordinances are approved.

  Mayor MAZA inquired if the City’s ordinance can supersede State regulations regarding
  concealed weapons. City Attorney MONTES responded to questions.

  Action Taken:  City Council took the following actions:

  1.  Adopted Ordinance No. O2M23-4818 entitled: AN URGENCY ORDINANCE OF THE
  CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA, CALIFORNIA, ENACTED
  PURSUANT TO CALIFORNIA GOVERNMENT CODE SECTION 65858, ADOPTING
  AN INTERIM ZONING ORDINANCE TEMPORARILY PROHIBITING THE
  ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW FIREARM SALES BUSINESSES IN THE CITY; and,

  2.  Approved the first reading of Ordinance No. O2M23-4819 entitled: AN ORDINANCE
  OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA, CALIFORNIA, ADDING
  SECTION 9.92.050 “SAFE STORAGE” TO THE ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE TO
  REQUIRE THE SAFE STORAGE OF FIREARMS; and,

  3.  Approved the first reading of Ordinance No O2M23-4820 entitled: AN ORDINANCE
  OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA, CALIFORNIA, ADDING
  CHAPTER 13.18 “FIREARMS PROHIBITED ON PUBLIC PROPERTY” TO THE
  ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE

  Vote:  Moved:  PÉREZ  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  MALONEY, LEE, PÉREZ, MAZA
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  ANDRADE-STADLER

 3.  AWARD CONTRACT: PROFESSIONAL ENGINEERING DESIGN SERVICES FOR THE
  GREEN STREET DEMONSTRATION STORMWATER CAPTURE PROJECT ON MAIN
  STREET – F2M23-56, RFP2M23-21, C2M23-77, M2M23-164

  On July 24, 2023, the City Council approved the distribution of a Request for Proposals for
  Engineering Design Services for the Green Street Demonstration Project on Main Street. A
  green street is a stormwater management approach that incorporates vegetation (perennials,
  shrubs, trees), soil, and engineered systems (e.g., permeable pavements) to slow, filter, and
  cleanse stormwater runoff from impervious surfaces (e.g., streets, sidewalks). There were
  three proposals received for the project. A review committee comprised of three staff members
  reviewed the submitted proposals. Staff evaluated the proposals based on qualifications,
  experience, references, technical approach, responsiveness and cost. CWE was selected as
  the most responsive firm.

  Public Comment:
  1) Bernice Ortega, 227 S. El Molina St., complemented the new temporary dog park and
  expressed concern with the location of the Green Street Project and its proximity to the City of
  Los Angeles.

  2) Lewis McCammon, 105 N. Cordova St., inquired if any of the water will be available as drinking
  water and complimented staff for information provided in Item No. 2.

  Discussion: Councilmember MALONEY expressed support for the Green Street project,
  expressed hope that more parts of the City will benefit from stormwater capture in the future,
  and hoped that the water captured can be utilized in the future as well.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language approval by
  the City Manager and City Attorney, by and between the City of Alhambra and CWE for
  Engineering Design Services for the Green Street Demonstration Project on Main Street in an
  amount not to exceed $580,800.00; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to
  finalize Council’s action. (M2M23-164)

  Vote:  Moved:  PÉREZ  Seconded:  MALONEY

5.  HUD 2022-2023 CONSOLIDATED ANNUAL PERFORMANCE AND EVALUATION
  REPORT (CAPER) – F2M7-84, M2M23-167

  Each year, the City of Alhambra is required by the Department of Housing and Urban
  Development to prepare a “Performance Report” for the CDBG and HOME programs. This
  report covers the previous fiscal year’s activities and expenditures. The report also highlights
  the accomplishments of the year and how the City is achieving progress with respect to the
  community development goals and objectives outlined in the One-Year Action Plan and the
  Five-Year Consolidated Plan. Staff requests that the City Council approve the 2022-2023
  Consolidated Annual Performance and Evaluation Report (CAPER) and direct staff to submit
  the report to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

7.  AWARD CONTRACT: TOPTRACER SERVICES PROGRAM – F2M22-49, C2M23-78,
  M2M23-168

  TOPTRACER Range, owned by TopGolf USA, features video monitors mounted in the
  traditional driving range bay. They are connected to cameras that track golf ball flight and
  replicate it on the screen, along with an array of statistics. On June 27, 2022, the City Council
  approved a 1-year agreement with TopGolf USA Inc.; however, the remaining years of this
  agreement were not executed due to ongoing price negotiations. Those negotiations have now
  been settled; therefore, staff is requesting the Council award a new 5-year agreement for the
  current equipment, plus the addition of TopTracer on the upper decks of the driving range as
  well. The addition of TOPTRACER equipment enhances and increases participation and
  revenue at the Alhambra Driving Range. TopGolf USA Inc. TOPTRACER is a sole-source
  service provider as it is a proprietary program.

  Discussion:  None

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language approval by
  the City Manager and the City Attorney, by and between the City of Alhambra and TopGolf
  USA Inc. for the installation and use of proprietary golf-ball tracking software, video monitors,
  and cameras in an amount not to exceed $376,294.20 commencing on July 1, 2023 through
  June 30, 2028; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.
  (M2M23-168)

COUNCIL COMMUNICATIONS (ANNOUNCEMENTS & FUTURE AGENDA ITEMS) – F2M23-7

Councilmember LEE discussed several community events over the summer months in the City and
thanked the staff for all their hard work putting on those events.

Councilmember MALONEY thanked those speakers who acknowledged the new temporary dog park,
discussed the comments made by Ms. Hosokawa and noted the City has a Human Relations
Committee that the community can reach out to for concerns, discussed regional and local discussions
and programs pertaining to Asian/Pacific Islander (API) hate, and noted that the City takes those
concerns very seriously.

Vice Mayor PÉREZ reiterated Councilmember MALONEY’s comments regarding API hate, discussed
a recent ride along with the Alhambra Police Department, and discussed the need for mental health
support in the Police Department.

Mayor MAZA suggested conducting future neighborhood watch meetings and signage to help combat
crimes against seniors, discussed the upcoming Compost Giveaway event, noted that the temporary
dog park will be open until November 5, 2023, stated there are free COVID-19 tests available at the
public library, discussed the upcoming Alhambra Recycles event, discussed the City’s annual Autumn
Fest event, and the annual Fire Department Open House event.
